questions.scenario: You are building a structured data extraction system using Claude. The system extracts information from unstructured documents, validates the output using JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) schemas, and maintains high accuracy. It must handle edge cases gracefully and integrate with downstream systems.
questions.stem: Low-confidence extractions now go to a review queue. Each item shows the full 12-page source document and the complete extracted JSON, and reviewers are asked to "approve or correct." An audit finds that reviewers approve 99% of items in under 20 seconds, and that many approved items still contained a wrong value in the very field that caused the flag. What change would MOST improve the value of the review step?

options.text: Add a mandatory comment box so that every approval requires a written justification, and reject any justification shorter than one full sentence.
Show each flagged field with its extracted value, the source snippet it came from and the flag reason, so reviewers verify that item.
Ask the model to re-check its own flagged extractions before they enter the queue, so reviewers see fewer items overall.
Hire additional reviewers so each person handles fewer items per day and can spend more time reading each document from start to finish.

questions.explanation: Review is only a control if it points human attention at **what is actually uncertain**. Field-level confidence exists so the reviewer knows *which field* to check. Showing the field, the source snippet and the reason for the flag turns a rubber stamp into a real verification step at almost no extra cost.

whyWrong.A: Extra friction produces boilerplate comments. It does not tell reviewers where to look, so the wrong field still gets approved.
whyWrong.C: Model self-review does not change what reviewers see and is not an independent check. It can quietly remove items from review without any measured accuracy.
whyWrong.D: More time on a 12-page document still leaves the reviewer hunting for the problem. Capacity is not the issue; the review design is.

questions.mindset: Make human review targeted: show the flagged field, its evidence and the reason, not the whole document.

questions.scenario: You are building a structured data extraction system using Claude. The system extracts information from unstructured documents, validates the output using JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) schemas, and maintains high accuracy. It must handle edge cases gracefully and integrate with downstream systems.
questions.stem: Reviewers correct about 300 extracted fields a week. Their corrections are written straight back to the finance system and are not used for anything else. Three months later the same kinds of errors are still being flagged at the same rate, and the confidence thresholds have never been revisited. Which change gives the MOST lasting improvement?

options.text: Raise every confidence threshold by 0.05 so that more fields are routed to review and more errors are caught before they reach the finance system.
Add a sentence to the prompt asking the model to take special care with the fields that reviewers correct most often.
Move the pipeline to the largest available model, since persistent error patterns of this kind usually mean the current model lacks capability.
Record each correction as structured data, add it to the labeled evaluation set, and use it to fix recurring patterns and recalibrate thresholds.

questions.explanation: Reviewer corrections are **free ground truth**. Recording them in structure (field, document type, original value, corrected value) lets the team find recurring error patterns, fix them in the prompt, schema or examples, measure the fix against an evaluation set that grows over time, and recalibrate thresholds. Without that loop, review only patches individual records.

whyWrong.A: An arbitrary threshold shift increases reviewer load without fixing any cause, and it is not based on measured accuracy.
whyWrong.B: A vague "take care" instruction doesn't address the specific failure patterns and gives no way to measure whether anything improved.
whyWrong.C: A bigger model is an unmeasured guess. Without an evaluation set built from the corrections, you can't tell whether it fixes these errors.

questions.mindset: Close the loop: human corrections should feed the eval set, the fixes and the thresholds.

questions.scenario: You are building a structured data extraction system using Claude. The system extracts information from unstructured documents, validates the output using JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) schemas, and maintains high accuracy. It must handle edge cases gracefully and integrate with downstream systems.
questions.stem: Extracted invoices feed an automated payments run. A calibration study shows that at confidence 0.85 or higher, vendor_name is 99.1% accurate and bank_account_number is 99.3% accurate. A wrong vendor name is cheap to fix later; a wrong account number sends money to the wrong party and is hard to recover. The team proposes one 0.85 threshold for all fields to keep the design simple. What is the BEST response?

options.text: Set thresholds per field by error cost: auto-approve vendor_name, but keep bank_account_number under review unless a stricter level is validated.
Accept the single threshold, because both fields measured above 99% accuracy and the calibration data shows that they behave almost identically.
Keep one threshold but raise it to 0.95 for every field, so the riskiest field is covered and the rule stays uniform.
Ask the model to report a high confidence for bank details only when it is highly certain, and keep the shared 0.85 threshold.

questions.explanation: Calibration tells you the **error rate**; the business decides what error rate is **acceptable**, and that depends on the consequence. A 0.7% error rate may be fine for a vendor name but not for an irreversible payment field. Thresholds (or mandatory review) should be set **per field**, using both the measured accuracy and the cost of a mistake.

whyWrong.B: Similar accuracy does not mean similar risk. A 0.7% error rate on account numbers means about 7 misdirected payments per 1,000, which could be unacceptable even though 99.3% sounds high.
whyWrong.C: A uniform 0.95 over-reviews low-risk fields and wastes capacity, and nobody has validated that 0.95 actually meets the bar needed for account numbers.
whyWrong.D: This is a prompt-only fix that changes what the score means without recalibrating it, so the existing calibration no longer applies.

questions.mindset: Thresholds come from measured accuracy and the cost of being wrong, per field.

questions.scenario: You are building a structured data extraction system using Claude. The system extracts information from unstructured documents, validates the output using JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) schemas, and maintains high accuracy. It must handle edge cases gracefully and integrate with downstream systems.
questions.stem: To calibrate confidence thresholds, the team has humans label 1,500 extractions. To save effort, they take all of them from the existing review queue, which only receives items the model scored below 0.8. They find accuracy rises steadily with confidence up to 0.8, conclude that scores above 0.8 are reliable, and automate those. What is the main flaw in this approach?

options.text: 1,500 labeled items is far too few to calibrate any threshold; calibration needs tens of thousands of examples per field before the error rates mean anything.
The reviewers who labeled the items also review production output every day, so their labels are not independent of the pipeline that is being measured.
The labeled set has no items above 0.8, so it says nothing about accuracy in the range being automated; sample the full confidence range instead.
Calibration should be done by having the model grade its own outputs against the source documents, which avoids the cost of human labeling.

questions.explanation: A calibration set must be **representative of the decisions it supports**. Drawing only from the low-confidence queue leaves the automated range (above 0.8) completely unmeasured, so the conclusion is an extrapolation, not evidence. Sample labeled items across the whole confidence range, and across document types and fields (stratified), before setting thresholds.

whyWrong.A: There is no universal minimum like this. 1,500 items can be enough if they cover the relevant range and segments; the problem here is *which* items were labeled, not the total.
whyWrong.B: Production reviewers are a normal source of ground-truth labels. Their labels are human judgments about the source documents, not outputs of the pipeline.
whyWrong.D: Model self-grading is not ground truth and cannot measure the model's own error rate. Human-verified labels are what calibration needs.

questions.mindset: Calibrate on a sample that covers the range you plan to automate, not just the items already flagged.

questions.scenario: You are building a structured data extraction system using Claude. The system extracts information from unstructured documents, validates the output using JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) schemas, and maintains high accuracy. It must handle edge cases gracefully and integrate with downstream systems.
questions.stem: Per-field thresholds were calibrated six months ago against a labeled set. In one release, the team now plans to move to a newer model and rewrite the extraction prompt. They want to carry the existing thresholds over unchanged, since "the newer model should be at least as good." What should they do?

options.text: Carry the thresholds over and rely on the existing stratified sample of auto-approved items to reveal any problems after the release goes live.
Re-run the labeled evaluation set on the new model and prompt, recalibrate each field's threshold, and only then switch routing over.
Lower every threshold slightly, because a stronger model should earn more automation, and review the effect at the next quarterly audit.
Ask the new model to state whether its confidence scores are calibrated the same way as the scores produced by the previous model.

questions.explanation: A threshold is calibrated for **one model and one prompt**. Changing either can shift both accuracy and how confidence scores are distributed. Re-running the existing labeled set is cheap and turns "should be at least as good" into evidence, before any extraction is auto-approved under the new setup.

whyWrong.A: Sampling after go-live catches problems late, after wrong values have already posted. Re-validation before rollout is cheap because the labeled set already exists.
whyWrong.C: This assumes improvement without measuring it. The new scores may be distributed differently, so a lower threshold could auto-approve more errors.
whyWrong.D: A model cannot report on its own calibration. Only comparison against ground truth can show it.

questions.mindset: Any change to model or prompt invalidates the calibration until you re-measure.

questions.stem: An invoice extraction pipeline sends fields to human review using only the model's self-reported confidence. Audits show some fields are wrong even at very high confidence. The team wants additional signals that catch these confident-but-wrong extractions without flooding reviewers. Which TWO signals are MOST useful to add to the routing logic? Choose TWO.

options.text: A deterministic check that fails when extracted line items do not add up to the extracted total, or when required fields contradict each other.
A second call that shows the model its own extracted JSON without the source document, asking it to confirm or revise each value before approval.
The length of the source document, routing every document above a fixed page count to human review regardless of the extracted values or their scores.
Flag items when several independent extraction runs of the same document disagree, comparing the runs field by field before anything is approved.
A system-prompt instruction telling the model to lower its confidence score whenever a field is hard to read in the source document.

questions.explanation: Good routing combines the model's score with **signals that don't depend on the model's opinion of itself**. Deterministic consistency checks (sums, cross-field rules) catch errors whatever the confidence. Comparing several independent runs (best-of-N) shows instability: if runs disagree on a field, it needs a human even when each run sounds sure.

whyWrong.B: Without the source document the model can only judge whether its own values look plausible. That is a second opinion from the same model, not independent evidence, and it will tend to confirm confident errors.
whyWrong.C: Page count is a crude proxy unrelated to whether a specific field is wrong. It floods the queue with correct long documents and misses short wrong ones.
whyWrong.E: This is still a self-report, now with an extra subjective rule. It is not calibrated, and confident errors are exactly the ones where the model doesn't think the field is hard.

questions.mindset: Back up self-reported confidence with independent signals: deterministic checks and cross-run agreement.

questions.stem: A labeled validation set contains 4,000 invoices but only 25 freight bills. All 25 freight bills were extracted correctly, each at high confidence. A manager now asks to automate freight bills along with invoices, pointing to the "perfect" result. What is the MOST appropriate response?

options.text: Automate them now, since a 100% accuracy result on every labeled item is the strongest evidence that this segment is safe to run without review.
Automate them, but add an instruction to the prompt asking the model to take extra care with freight bills from now on.
Merge freight bills into the invoice segment, so that the much larger invoice sample size covers both document types in one measurement.
Keep freight bills under human review, and grow the labeled sample for that segment until its accuracy can be established with confidence.

questions.explanation: 25 correct results is too small a sample to show that the error rate is low enough to remove review: even a segment with a meaningful error rate could easily produce 25 correct items in a row. Keep the segment under review (which also produces the labels you need) until the per-segment sample is large enough to support the decision.

whyWrong.A: A perfect score on a tiny sample is weak evidence. The uncertainty around the true error rate is still wide.
whyWrong.B: A prompt instruction does not create evidence of accuracy. The segment would be automated with no measured basis.
whyWrong.C: Merging hides the segment inside the invoice average, which is exactly how weak segments get missed.

questions.mindset: Automate a segment only when its own sample is big enough to trust.

questions.scenario: You are building a customer support resolution agent using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent handles high-ambiguity requests like returns, billing disputes, and account issues. It has access to your backend systems through custom Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human). Your target is 80%+ first-contact resolution while knowing when to escalate.
questions.stem: The team wants humans in the loop but cannot review every conversation without missing the first-contact resolution target. The agent's actions range from reading account details and sending order-status updates to issuing refunds through process_refund, including occasional large refunds that cannot be recovered. Which review design is MOST appropriate?

options.text: Require a supervisor to approve every agent reply before it is sent, so no action happens without human sign-off, whatever its size or reversibility.
Review a random sample of closed conversations every week, and use the findings to update the prompt, for all action types equally.
Require human approval, enforced in code, before refunds above a set amount execute, and use sampled after-the-fact review for low-risk, reversible actions.
Have the agent state in each reply how confident it is before a refund, and let supervisors read those notes during weekly sampled reviews.

questions.explanation: Match the **timing** of review to the **risk**. Irreversible, high-value actions need approval *before* they execute, and that gate should be deterministic (for example a hook or permission callback on process_refund), not a prompt instruction. Reversible, low-risk actions can run automatically and be checked by sampling afterwards, which keeps resolution rates high.

whyWrong.A: Approving every reply makes humans the bottleneck, ruins the resolution target and leads to rubber-stamping because reviewers are overloaded.
whyWrong.B: After-the-fact review cannot undo an irreversible refund, and treating all actions equally ignores where the real risk is.
whyWrong.D: Self-reported confidence is uncalibrated, and reading it a week later does not prevent anything.

questions.mindset: Gate irreversible actions before they happen; sample reversible ones afterwards.

questions.stem: After calibration, 40% of all extracted fields are routed to review, far beyond reviewer capacity, and the backlog keeps growing. Analysis shows that two-thirds of routed fields are one field, payment_terms, which documents phrase in many different ways, and that thresholds were set as one global value rather than per field. Which TWO actions BEST reduce the review load without lowering reliability? Choose TWO.

options.text: Lower the global threshold until the routed volume matches reviewer capacity, then keep monitoring quality with the existing random sample of auto-approved items.
Calibrate thresholds per field against the labeled set, so fields that are accurate at lower confidence stop being routed to review.
Auto-approve backlog items after a fixed waiting period, since a review that arrives weeks late has little remaining value for the downstream finance system.
Remove payment_terms from the extraction schema, so the model no longer extracts the field that causes most of the review load.
Fix the extraction of payment_terms itself, with a clearer field definition, normalized values and examples of varied phrasings, and then re-measure.

questions.explanation: Two levers reduce review load **without** accepting more errors: (1) **per-field calibration**, because a single global threshold over-routes fields that are reliable at lower scores; (2) **fixing the extraction itself** for the field that dominates the queue, then re-measuring. Both reduce volume based on evidence, not on capacity.

whyWrong.A: This sets the threshold from reviewer capacity instead of measured accuracy, so it silently auto-approves more wrong fields.
whyWrong.C: Time-based auto-approval ships unreviewed, low-confidence data. It removes the control exactly where it is needed.
whyWrong.D: Dropping a field the business needs is not a reliability fix. It just moves the problem downstream.

questions.mindset: Cut review volume with per-field calibration and root-cause fixes, never by lowering the bar to fit capacity.

questions.stem: A compliance tool needs two things for each answer about uploaded policy documents: a strict JSON record for the case-management system, and verifiable pointers to the exact supporting passages. A developer enables Citations on the document blocks and also sets a JSON schema output format on the same request, and the API rejects the call. What is the BEST way to meet both requirements?

options.text: Keep Citations on the grounded-answer request, and build the JSON record in code (or a separate step) from the response's text and citation blocks.
Drop Citations and add a source_quote string field to the JSON schema, asking the model to copy each claim's exact supporting passage into that field.
Keep the JSON schema and instruct the model in the prompt to include page numbers for every claim, then store the numbers it returns.
Retry the combined request with a larger max_tokens value, because the rejection is caused by the extra output space that the citation blocks need.

questions.explanation: Citations and structured outputs **cannot be combined on one request**: enabling citations on a document block together with a JSON schema output format returns a 400 error, because citations interleave citation blocks with text, which conflicts with strict schema constraints. Citations give pointers that are guaranteed to be valid references into the supplied documents, which is what auditors need. Keep that call, then produce the strict JSON from its text and citation blocks in code or in a separate structured step.

whyWrong.B: A model-written quote field has no guarantee that it matches the document. It may be paraphrased or wrong, which loses the verifiability the auditors require.
whyWrong.C: Prompted page numbers are not validated against the document, so they can point to the wrong place. This is a prompt-only fix where a built-in mechanism exists.
whyWrong.D: The incompatibility is by design, not a token limit. Increasing max_tokens will not make the combined request valid.

questions.mindset: Keep provenance mechanical: let the API produce citations, then shape the record in code.

questions.stem: A team uses Citations to answer questions about meeting transcripts, which they send as plain-text documents. Reviewers complain that cited passages are cut at sentence boundaries that don't line up with speaker turns, so it is often hard to tell who said what. Each transcript is already stored as a list of speaker turns. What is the MOST effective change?

options.text: Add a prompt instruction telling the model to name the speaker before it quotes anything from the transcript in its answer.
Convert each transcript to a PDF, so that citations come back with page numbers that reviewers can look up in the original file.
Send each transcript as a custom content document with one content block per speaker turn, so that each citation points to a whole turn.
Turn off Citations and ask the model to reproduce the relevant transcript lines in full at the end of each answer it gives.

questions.explanation: Plain-text and PDF documents are chunked into sentences automatically. **Custom content documents** use your content blocks as-is, so citations refer to the blocks you defined. One block per speaker turn makes each citation map to a whole, attributable turn, which suits transcripts.

whyWrong.A: The model's mention of a speaker is not tied to the citation, so it can be wrong, and the cited span is still cut at sentence boundaries.
whyWrong.B: Page numbers are coarser, not more precise, and still do not line up with speaker turns.
whyWrong.D: This gives up guaranteed-valid pointers for model-reproduced text that might be inaccurate.

questions.mindset: Control citation granularity by how you structure the source, not by prompting.

questions.scenario: You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents: one searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes findings, and one generates reports. The system researches topics and produces comprehensive, cited reports.
questions.stem: Subagent outputs now carry claim-source mappings, but reviewers still find fluent claims in the final reports that have no source attached. Traces show that the synthesis subagent fills gaps between findings with background statements from its own general knowledge. What is the MOST effective fix?

options.text: Ask the synthesis subagent to write in a more cautious tone, so that unsourced sentences read as general background context rather than as research findings.
Restrict the synthesizer to the supplied findings, have it verify every claim against a source excerpt, and flag or remove unsupported ones.
Have the report-generation subagent append a numbered bibliography at the end, listing every source consulted during the research run with its URL and title.
Increase the number of search results each web-search subagent retrieves, so fewer gaps are left for the synthesizer to fill from its own knowledge.

questions.explanation: The provenance break is at the synthesis step, so fix it there: **restrict the synthesizer to the supplied findings** and add a **claim-by-claim verification** in which every statement must point to a supporting excerpt, and any that can't is removed or clearly flagged.

whyWrong.A: A softer tone hides unsupported claims instead of removing them. Readers still can't trace them.
whyWrong.C: A bibliography, even one listing every source with its URL and title, doesn't link any specific claim to a source, so unsourced claims remain impossible to verify.
whyWrong.D: More results may reduce some gaps, but the synthesizer will still fill whatever gaps remain with unsourced knowledge.

questions.mindset: Every claim in the output needs a traceable source; retract the ones that don't have one.

questions.scenario: You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents: one searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes findings, and one generates reports. The system researches topics and produces comprehensive, cited reports.
questions.stem: A report labels a statistic as "well established" because four sources report it. A reviewer notices that all four are news articles quoting the same vendor press release. The subagents' structured outputs record each article's URL, title and publication date. What change BEST prevents this kind of error in future reports?

options.text: Require at least six agreeing sources, rather than four, before any finding can be labeled as well established anywhere in the report.
Tell the synthesis subagent to prefer academic sources over news articles whenever both kinds of source are available for a claim.
Remove news articles from the search results entirely, so that only primary documents ever reach the synthesis step of the pipeline.
Have subagents also record the original upstream source that each item relies on, and count corroboration by independent origins rather than by URLs.

questions.explanation: Corroboration means **independent** evidence. Four articles repeating one press release are one source, not four. Recording the **originating source** in the claim-source mapping lets the synthesizer de-duplicate by origin and label the claim honestly ("single vendor source, widely reported").

whyWrong.A: Six articles repeating the same release would pass this rule too. The count is not the issue; independence is.
whyWrong.B: Source-type preference doesn't detect shared origins, and academic papers can also all rely on one dataset.
whyWrong.C: This throws away useful reporting and coverage, and primary documents can still repeat each other.

questions.mindset: Count independent origins, not copies, when judging how established a claim is.

questions.scenario: You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents: one searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes findings, and one generates reports. The system researches topics and produces comprehensive, cited reports.
questions.stem: One research sub-question, regional adoption in Southeast Asia, returned no usable sources. The final report still includes a confident regional adoption figure that no subagent found. What should the system do instead?

options.text: State in the report that no reliable source was found for that sub-question, and mark it clearly as a gap instead of giving a figure.
Have the synthesizer estimate a figure from neighbouring regions and show it in the same table as the figures that were sourced.
Quietly remove that sub-question from the report outline, so that readers are not distracted by the adoption figures that are missing.
Keep the figure but describe it as "approximately" in the report, so the reader understands that it is less precise than others.

questions.explanation: When evidence is missing, the honest output is **an explicit gap**. Allowing the model to say "I don't have enough information" is a basic way to reduce hallucinations, and a visible gap tells decision-makers where more research is needed.

whyWrong.B: An estimate shown next to sourced figures looks like a finding. It invents data and hides that it's unsourced.
whyWrong.C: Silently dropping the question hides a coverage gap the reader needs to know about.
whyWrong.D: "Approximately" suggests a measured value with some error, but here there is no source at all.

questions.mindset: Report missing evidence as a gap; never fill it with a plausible number.

questions.stem: Executives say the research briefs are cluttered by long source details after every sentence, and they ask for the sources to be removed. Analysts who act on the same briefs still need to check where each figure came from, and executives often forward figures from the brief to the board. What is the BEST approach?

options.text: Remove the sources from the executive version, and keep a separate copy with full sources on a shared drive for the analysts.
Keep sources only for the figures that the model considers surprising, and drop the source details for all of the other claims.
Use short inline reference markers in the text that link to a sources section listing each source with its excerpt and date.
Replace the individual sources with a single closing statement that the brief was produced from reputable industry and government publications.

questions.explanation: Readability and traceability are compatible. **Compact inline markers plus a sources section** keep the text clean while every figure stays traceable, including when an executive forwards it.

whyWrong.A: Two versions drift apart, and figures forwarded from the executive copy lose their provenance.
whyWrong.B: "Surprising" is a subjective model judgment. Ordinary-looking figures can be just as wrong and still need to be traceable.
whyWrong.D: A blanket statement makes no claim traceable, so it removes provenance completely.

questions.mindset: Make provenance light to read, not absent.

questions.stem: A document-analysis subagent summarizes papers for a synthesizer. One source is a preprint saying a treatment "may reduce symptoms in a small pilot (n=24)." The final report says the treatment "reduces symptoms." Which TWO changes BEST preserve the original level of certainty through the pipeline? Choose TWO.

options.text: Tell the report-generation subagent to put "studies suggest" in front of medical claims, so that the tone of the report is consistently cautious.
Have the subagent's structured output carry the source's own qualifiers and evidence details (study type, sample size, review status) with each claim.
Exclude preprints from the pipeline entirely, so that only peer-reviewed findings can ever reach the final report, and note the exclusion in the methodology.
Instruct the synthesizer to restate each claim at no more than the source's stated strength of evidence, keeping qualifiers such as "may" and "pilot".
Ask the synthesizer to give each claim a 1-10 confidence score based on how plausible the claim sounds, printed beside the claim.

questions.explanation: Hedges are lost during **compression**. Fix it at both ends: the summarizing subagent must **carry qualifiers and evidence metadata as structured fields**, and the synthesizer must **restate claims at the source's own strength**, never upgrading "may reduce" in a pilot to "reduces".

whyWrong.A: Hedging claims uniformly erases the difference between strong and weak evidence, which is exactly the information readers need.
whyWrong.C: Excluding preprints loses relevant evidence. The aim is to carry its strength through honestly, not to hide it.
whyWrong.E: Plausibility is not evidence. A gut-feel score is uncalibrated and ignores what the source actually says.

questions.mindset: Carry each source's own certainty forward; don't let summarization upgrade a 'may' to an 'is'.

questions.scenario: You are building developer productivity tools using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent helps engineers explore unfamiliar codebases, understand legacy systems, generate boilerplate code, and automate repetitive tasks. It uses the built-in tools (Read, Write, Bash, Grep, Glob) and integrates with Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers.
questions.stem: Engineers use the agent to explain a legacy billing module. Its summary says that calculate_late_fee "is only called from the nightly batch job." An engineer relies on this, changes the function, and breaks a call made through a dynamically built handler name that a text search would never match. Which TWO changes BEST make the agent's explanations safe to act on? Choose TWO.

options.text: Require each structural claim to cite the evidence it rests on, such as file paths and line numbers or the exact search that was run.
Have the agent phrase all of its claims in tentative language, so that engineers are reminded not to treat any part of a summary as fully reliable.
Label each claim as verified (read the proving code) or inferred (from names or searches), noting blind spots such as dynamic dispatch.
Move the agent to a larger model so that it can recognise dynamically built call sites from context without having to run any extra searches.
Limit the agent to summarizing one file at a time, so that it does not make claims about call sites that are located in other files.

questions.explanation: Provenance applies to code analysis too. **Cite the evidence** (files, lines, searches) so engineers can check a claim, and **separate verified facts from inferences**, naming known blind spots such as dynamic dispatch. "Only called from X" based on a grep is an inference and should be presented as one.

whyWrong.B: Hedging everything equally gives engineers no way to tell solid findings from guesses.
whyWrong.D: Model size doesn't make a text search complete, and engineers still couldn't tell how the claim was reached.
whyWrong.E: This avoids the problem by removing useful cross-file analysis. It doesn't make the claims that remain any more traceable.

questions.mindset: Show the evidence and say whether a claim is verified or inferred.

questions.scenario: You are building a customer support resolution agent using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent handles high-ambiguity requests like returns, billing disputes, and account issues. It has access to your backend systems through custom Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human). Your target is 80%+ first-contact resolution while knowing when to escalate.
questions.stem: The agent answers return-policy questions from retrieved knowledge-base articles. For one customer, two retrieved articles conflict: one says returns are accepted within 30 days, the other says 14 days. The retrieved text includes no effective dates, and the agent chose the 30-day article. What is the MOST reliable fix?

options.text: Instruct the agent to quote the more generous of the two policies whenever articles conflict, to protect customer satisfaction scores.
Retrieve each article with its effective date, answer from the version currently in effect and cite it, and escalate conflicts it cannot resolve.
Instruct the agent to prefer whichever article appears first in the search results, since the retrieval system ranks results by relevance.
Give the customer both figures and explain that the return window is either 14 or 30 days, depending on which article is correct.

questions.explanation: Conflicts like this are usually **version** problems, and they can only be resolved if provenance metadata (effective date, status) travels with the content. With that metadata the agent can answer from the version in effect and cite it. If the conflict still can't be resolved, it should escalate or flag it for content owners instead of guessing.

whyWrong.A: An arbitrary rule may commit the business to a policy that no longer applies, and it ignores what is actually in effect.
whyWrong.C: Relevance ranking says nothing about which policy is current. This is still an arbitrary pick.
whyWrong.D: Customers need a definitive answer. Passing an internal content conflict on to them is unhelpful; the business has to resolve it.

questions.mindset: Resolve conflicts with provenance metadata such as effective dates; escalate when that isn't enough.
